prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level
for the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the founding of neutrino astronomy with the IceCube detector

statement.case_for: I keep two discoveries at the centre of my view. B003 is a new window on the universe: the IceCube diffuse flux of TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrinos is a clean, original discovery, now confirmed by independent analyses and channels and strengthened by the TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane results. B022 is the other discovery I rank highly: the magic-wavelength lattice clock is a concrete, reproduced invention that took frequency metrology to the 10^-18 level and underpins tests of relativity and fundamental constants, a possible redefinition of the second and relativistic geodesy. B022 also has the cleanest attribution on the table (Katori proposed it, Ye brought it to the accuracy frontier), and with five top-three rankings from members across fields it has real breadth of support. Pairing a precision-measurement achievement with an observational discovery in astroparticle physics gives a two-part prize of three people and respects the breadth of physics.
statement.case_against: The weakest part is B003: a collaboration-scale discovery credited to a single name, with AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal pioneers and many IceCube builders and analysts outside the supplied credit, and most of the diffuse flux still has no identified source. Only Mark Pearce and I ranked it at all, so I cannot claim committee-wide support for it. B022 has its own reservation: it sits close to the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Finally, B039 has the strongest opening support (three first places, five top-three), and a prize that omits it must justify why the field's best-supported candidate is deferred.

responses.point: Pearce also ranks B003 first, but stresses that a one-name award for a collaboration-scale discovery is a thin and arguably unfair summary of the credit, and that independent confirmation from a second large detector is still limited.
responses.response: I agree that the single-name credit is the main weakness and I do not think it can be waved away. I still think the discovery is secure because IceCube's own independent channels agree, and the committee decides on the achievement, not on a roster. Where we may differ is how much weight the missing second-detector confirmation deserves: I see it as a point about future refinement, not about whether the flux exists. If you judge the attribution too thin to carry a part of the prize, I would rather hear that explicitly, because then B022 or B039 should stand alone.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B022 first as a clean and powerful use of laser spectroscopy whose impact reaches the redefinition of the second, geodesy and dark-matter searches, and notes that the lattice-clock idea is distinct from the comb and ion-clock lineage already honoured.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case and with the two-name attribution. On the earlier-prize overlap I would go further: the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a tool and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions, whereas the lattice clock is a new route to many-atom clocks with their own many-body physics. Your point that the redefinition of the second is pending is a fair caution, but I would treat it as a timing argument that cuts both ways rather than as a flaw. I also note that you rank B039 last of your list, which suggests it is not only condensed-matter members who see it as less central.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B039 first as a new classification of electronic phases by band topology, a clear theory-to-experiment chain from Kane-Mele through HgTe to Molenkamp, mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I accept that B039 is scientifically strong, and I raised it to the status of my main alternative after reading the discussion. I still have two reservations that I think the first-place supporters understate: the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases, so the committee must be clear what is new, and the credit problem is real, with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 3D work of Fu, Moore and Hasan, outside the three names. I do not accept that three first places make it the consensus pick by themselves; support is concentrated among condensed-matter members, and Kroll ranked it eighth.

responses.point: Mehlig sets out B039 as a conceptually clean invariant-based classification that spread to photonics and cold atoms, and warns that the boundary of the discovery (2D quantum spin Hall versus 3D topological insulators) is uncertain.
responses.response: Your boundary question is exactly what I find hardest, and I agree it cannot be settled from the supplied names. I would add one observation: Zhang died in 2018, so the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit is partly moot for the prize, but Bernevig and Hughes remain, and the 3D discoverers are living. If the committee wants B039, it should say plainly whether the citation is for the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or for topological insulators broadly, and I would want that settled before I relax my reservation.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B022 first and B039 second, valuing the elegant and decisive lattice-clock idea backed by precise atomic-structure input, and regards the clock as a later achievement separate from the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I agree on both points and it moves me towards putting B022 first in a pairing. Your concern that ion-clock groups and other lattice-clock groups are not covered by the supplied credit is a fair attribution limit, but I think the Katori-Ye pair captures the concept and the accuracy frontier. I disagree only mildly with ranking B039 so close behind: your own note that its practical applications remain limited makes me prefer to pair the clock with a discovery that opens a new observational channel.

uncertainties: Whether a one-name award for B003 can be defended given the collaboration nature of IceCube and the omission of AMANDA/DUMAND pioneers.
Whether the committee wants B039 as the single most-supported candidate, and if so whether the citation is for 2D quantum spin Hall or topological insulators broadly.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay B022.
How much the 2016 topological-phase prize and the 2012 and 2025 prizes in related areas should reduce room for B039, B005 and B023.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: my documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is a credited name on any shortlisted ballot.
